findings.title: Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware wrapper, so updates can be silently skipped
findings.body:
`update()` obtains `original` from `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is on) returns the anonymous wrapper created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, while `updated` is the raw model. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` therefore compares a model whose enabled state depends on *external* org state against a raw model, and bails out of invalidating when both sides fail the login predicate.

Concrete failure: organization X is disabled; IDP `idp1` is linked to X with `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`, raw `enabled=true`, `hideOnLogin=false`. The login caches were populated from the JPA query (which filters on the raw DB columns), so `idp1`'s id is in the `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` entries. An admin now sets `hideOnLogin=true`: `test(original)` is false (org disabled ⇒ wrapper reports disabled) and `test(updated)` is false (hidden), so the first early-return triggers and no login cache is invalidated. When organization X is re-enabled, `getForLogin` keeps returning `idp1`'s id and `getById` returns a non-null model, so the IDP that is explicitly hidden on login is rendered on the login page (the bean only re-checks `isEnabled()`, not `hideOnLogin`/`linkOnly`).

Use the unwrapped model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`) or compare the raw fields (`enabled`, `linkOnly`, `hideOnLogin`, `organizationId`, `BROKER_PUBLIC`) when deciding whether to invalidate. Note `remove()` correctly uses the raw delegate model, so the two paths are inconsistent today. There is also no test covering a disabled organization combined with a cached login list.

findings.title: Single per-realm login cache entry keyed by organizationId is rebuilt/invalidated for every unseen organization
findings.body:
`getForLogin` uses one cache key per realm+FetchMode (`cacheKeyForLogin`) and stores the per-organization result sets inside a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` under `searchKey = organizationId`. When a request arrives with an organizationId that is not yet present in that entry, the code calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` (bumping the revision) and re-adds a merged query containing all previously cached search keys plus the new one.

On the login hot path this means: (a) the first login for each of N organizations in a realm invalidates and rebuilds the shared entry, so the realm's login IDP lookup is re-queried and the entry re-serialized O(N) times, and concurrent first-logins for different orgs will repeatedly drop each other's entry and re-hit the DB; (b) the entry grows monotonically with the number of organizations, so a realm with thousands of orgs ends up with one very large cache object that the realm cache's eviction policy treats as a single element. For `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the problem is gratuitous: `organizationId` is ignored by the query, yet it is still used as `searchKey`, so each distinct org id creates another identical result set (and another invalidate/rebuild cycle). Consider putting the organization id in the Infinispan key itself, or at least using a constant search key for `REALM_ONLY`.

findings.title: Cleanup registers the literal alias "alias", so the 21 IDPs created by the new test are never removed
findings.body:
`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425) references a hard-coded alias `"alias"` instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). At cleanup time the admin client targets a non-existent provider, so either the cleanup throws `NotFoundException` or it silently does nothing; in both cases none of the 21 identity providers created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are deleted, and `idp-alias-20` stays linked to organization `orga`.

Because the test realm is imported once per class, this leaks state into the other methods of this class: `testCacheIDPByOrg` asserts exact counts (`assertEquals(6, ...)`, `assertEquals(2/4, ...)`) for the IDPs of orga/orgb, and `testCacheIDPForLogin` itself asserts exact counts (5/5/10, 6/5/11, 5/6/11) that are only valid in a clean realm. Depending on JUnit's method order, one of the two tests will fail or produce misleading results. (The same mistake exists in the pre-existing line 303 and should be fixed there too.)
